author: reek
body: A subdirectory that has run out of slots grows a cluster instead of refusing a write the volume has room for.

author: reek
body: Fourteen-then-one is deliberate. A test that wrote fifteen files and checked only the count would pass on a volume that grew on the first write and on one that never needed to, so it would not be evidence about growth at all. The fill is sized to leave the directory exactly full, which makes the next write the first one that cannot be served without a new cluster.

author: reek
body: The chain length is the direct evidence. SUB is resolved and its cluster chain is walked through the FAT: one cluster before the fifteenth file, two after. A write that reported True while quietly landing the entry somewhere else would not move this number.

author: reek
body: The read-back of the FIRST file is what catches a growth that corrupts what was already there. The new cluster is zeroed before it is linked, and the link is written last; if either were done in the other order, an existing entry or a stale one would show up here.

author: reek
body: F15 must NOT be in the root. A writer that gave up on the parent and fell back to the root would report True and read back through SUB/ correctly if the walk found it there -- reading the root is what tells those apart, the same way fat16-subdir pins it.

author: reek
body: Each write allocates a cluster for the file's own bytes as well as taking a slot, so this exercises the allocator fourteen times over before the directory itself needs anything.

author: reek
body: The walk stops on anything a chain cannot continue into, not only on the end-of-chain marker, so a corrupt volume ends this loop rather than hanging the machine.
